title: Core of the Truehearted 9
content:
Mid-sentence, he reached out, grabbed two sturdy branches, and began hauling himself up the trunk. He scrambled upward with practiced ease, only coming to a halt near the leafy crown. "Yep, right about here, I'd say."

Burying his face in the thick cluster of leaves for a lingering moment, he finally peeked down. His voice floated down from high above, light and laced with a teasing laugh. "Felt terrifyingly high back then. Looking down now, it's really not that bad."

The second his arms had wrapped around the rough bark, heat rushed behind his eyes. By the time he peered downward, his vision was already a blurred smear.

Lan Wangji stood straight beneath the boughs, head tilted up to track him. Clad entirely in white, he carried no paper lantern. Yet moonlight seemed to pool and silver across his frame, draping him in a soft, ethereal radiance. He kept his chin tipped up, eyes fixed intently on the canopy. Taking a few measured steps closer to the trunk, he looked as though he were on the verge of lifting his hands.

All at once, a reckless, overwhelming impulse flared in Wei Wuxian’s chest.

He wanted to fall. Just like back then. One more time.

A voice in his head whispered: If he catches me, I'll...

The second the thought I'll crossed his mind, he let go.

Seeing him tumble out of the leaves without warning, Lan Wangji’s eyes went wide. He surged forward in a blinding lunge—and caught him dead-center. Or rather, Wei Wuxian crashed full-tilt straight into his chest.

Lan Wangji was built lean and slender, the picture of an aristocratic gentleman, but his strength was terrifying. Beyond iron wrists and incredible arm power, his balance was immovable. Still, taking the deadweight of a full-grown man plummeting out of a tree knocked even him back by half a pace. He swayed on his heels for a split second, then planted his boots firmly into the dirt.

He moved to set Wei Wuxian down, only to find two arms looped stubbornly around his neck, locking him tight in place.

Lan Wangji couldn't see his face, and Wei Wuxian couldn't see his. But neither needed to look. Eyes shut tight, all Wei Wuxian could breathe in was the cool, grounding scent of sandalwood radiating from Lan Wangji's robes.

His voice came out a quiet, raspy scrape: "Thanks."

He wasn't afraid of falling. Over the years, he’d kissed the dirt plenty of times. But hitting the ground still hurt like hell.

Having someone there to catch you—there was truly nothing better.

Having someone there to catch you was infinitely better.

At the quiet murmur of thanks, Lan Wangji's shoulders seemed to stiffen. The hand he had moved to rest against Wei Wuxian's back hovered, hesitated, and ultimately dropped back down.

After a beat of heavy silence, Lan Wangji murmured, "No need."

They clung to each other for what felt like an eternity before Wei Wuxian finally pulled away. Standing tall again, he puffed his chest out like nothing had happened. "Come on, let's head back!"

"Done sightseeing?"

"For now!" Wei Wuxian chuckled. "Nothing else out here to see anyway—keep walking and it's just barren weeds, and we've had our fill of those lately. Let's go back inside Lotus Pier. There's one last spot I want to show you."

Tracing their steps back toward the water, they slipped back past the front gates. Cutting across the sprawling training grounds, Wei Wuxian slowed to a halt outside a lavish pavilion, his gaze lingering on the timber with an unreadable look.

Lan Wangji asked, "What is it?"

Wei Wuxian shook his head. "Nothing. My old room used to sit right here. Gone now—torn down, just like I thought. All these structures are brand new."

Winding past the labyrinth of pristine buildings, they tucked deep into a secluded, quiet corner of the estate, coming to a stop before a somber, black octagonal hall. As if terrified of waking a sleeping ghost, Wei Wuxian nudged the heavy doors open with a gentle push and stepped inside. Facing the entrance stood row upon row of neatly arranged wooden memorial tablets.

The ancestral shrine of the Yunmeng Jiang Clan.

He grabbed a prayer mat and dropped to his knees, pulling three incense sticks from the altar box. Striking them against a candle flame until the tips glowed amber, he planted them firmly into the bronze brazier before two specific tablets. He bowed deeply three times, turning back toward Lan Wangji with an easy grin. "Used to be a regular in this hall."

Lan Wangji’s expression softened with quiet understanding. "Punished with kneeling?"

Wei Wuxian blinked. "How'd you know? Spot on. Madam Yu had me in here kneeling every other day."

Lan Wangji inclined his head. "I had heard."

"If gossip from Yunmeng carried all the way to Gusu, that's a bit more than 'heard'!" Wei Wuxian laughed. "Though to be totally fair, I've never met another woman with a temper as foul as Madam Yu’s. Any tiny mistake and it was: 'Get your ass to the shrine and kneel!' Hahaha..."

Yet, looking back... beyond all the screaming and scolding, Madam Yu had never actually done anything to truly harm him.

Realizing where he was standing—with Madam Yu’s very tablet staring him down—he winced, frantically muttering, "My bad, my bad!" To atone for running his mouth, he lit three fresh incense sticks, hoisting them high above his head while murmuring apologies under his breath.

A shadow fell over his side. Glancing over, Lan Wangji had quietly dropped to his knees beside him.

Etiquette demanded respect in an ancestral hall, and Lan Wangji was nothing if not proper. He took three sticks of his own, tucked his sleeve back to light them against a red taper, and held them with pristine, solemn poise. Wei Wuxian watched him from the corner of his eye, the edges of his mouth curving upward on their own.

Lan Wangji cast a quiet glance his way. "The ash."

Wei Wuxian’s incense had been burning for a while, a fragile gray curl of ash threatening to tumble from the tip. Yet he made no move to plant them into the burner, straightening his spine with sudden, deadpan earnestness. "Together."

Lan Wangji offered no objection. Side by side, each holding their three sticks high, they knelt before the ancestral ranks and touched their foreheads to the floorboards, bowing in unison before the carved names of Jiang Fengmian and Yu Ziyuan.

Once. Twice. Their movements mirrored each other down to the fraction of an inch.

"Done," Wei Wuxian murmured. Only then did he reverently slide the incense into the bronze tripod.

Settling back on his knees, Wei Wuxian stole a peek at the razor-straight posture of the man beside him. Bringing his palms together in prayer, he silently whispered in his heart:

Uncle Jiang, Madam Yu, it's me again. Sorry for crashing your peace and quiet.

I just... I really wanted to bring this person here for you to see. Those two bows just now can count as bowing to Heaven and Earth, and bowing to parents. You two keep this man locked down for me first, alright? The final bow to each other—I'll put that on my tab for now, and make it up later...

A harsh, icy scoff shattered the silence from the doorway.

Caught mid-prayer, Wei Wuxian jolted, his eyes snapping open. Looking back over his shoulder, Jiang Cheng stood in the courtyard just outside the threshold, arms crossed tightly across his chest.

His voice drifted into the shrine, dripping pure frost: "Wei Wuxian, you really don't bother treating yourself like a guest, do you? Coming and going as you please, dragging whoever you want through my halls. Have you forgotten whose roof you're standing under? Who the master of this house is?"

Wei Wuxian had deliberately crept out here to avoid a run-in; getting caught red-handed meant an earful of bile was inevitable. Wanting to nip the spat in the bud, he replied, "I didn't bring Hanguang-jun anywhere near your restricted grounds. We just came to light incense for Uncle Jiang and Madam Yu. We're done. We're leaving."

"The further, the better," Jiang Cheng spat. "Don't let me catch your shadow crawling around Lotus Pier ever again!"

Wei Wuxian’s brow twitched. Catching sight of Lan Wangji’s right hand drifting toward the hilt of his sword, Wei Wuxian hurriedly reached out, clamping his fingers over Lan Wangji's knuckles.

Lan Wangji looked straight at Jiang Cheng, his tone flat: "Watch your tongue."

"I suggest the two of you watch your conduct first," Jiang Cheng fired right back, giving zero quarter.

The headache behind Wei Wuxian’s temples throbbed harder, a foul premonition twisting in his gut. He tugged at Lan Wangji's sleeve. "Hanguang-jun, let's go."

Turning back toward the altar, Wei Wuxian knocked his forehead against the floorboards a few more times with solemn reverence before rising to his feet alongside Lan Wangji.

Jiang Cheng didn't stop the bows, but his sneer deepened. "You should kneel to them. Showing your face here just to foul their sight and drag dirt across their rest."

Wei Wuxian swept a tired look over him. "We just lit some incense. Can you drop it?"

"Just lit some incense?" Jiang Cheng scoffed, taking a menacing step forward. "Wei Wuxian, do you have zero self-awareness left?! You were thrown out of this family years ago! What right do you have to drag random garbage into our ancestral shrine to burn incense for my parents?!"

Wei Wuxian had already begun brushing past him, but that single word made him freeze in his tracks. He turned slowly, his voice dangerously low: "Say that again. Who are you calling 'random garbage'?"

If he were standing here alone, Jiang Cheng could have spit in his face and he would have swallowed it without a blink. But Lan Wangji was standing right beside him. No matter what, he refused to let Lan Wangji stand there and take Jiang Cheng’s vile barbs and unchecked vitriol.

Jiang Cheng’s lip curled in bitter mockery. "Look at that, selective memory? Wondering who counts as garbage? Let me remind you. It was all because you had to play the big hero and save that Second Young Master Lan beside you that Lotus Pier burned to ash! My parents were dragged into the dirt to pay for your noble crusade! And that wasn't enough for you, was it? Once wasn't enough—you had to turn around and do it all over again, sticking your neck out for Wen dogs, dragging my sister and her husband straight into their graves! Look at you, aren't you magnificent? And look at your boundless grace today—parading both of them right into Lotus Pier! Leaving a Wen dog lurking outside my gates, bringing Second Young Master Lan inside to burn incense—you're doing this on purpose just to rub salt in my wounds!"

Jiang Cheng’s eyes burned with incandescent fury. "Wei Wuxian, who the hell do you think you are?! Who gave you the audacity to drag your pack into my family’s shrine?!"

Wei Wuxian had known this was coming. He knew Jiang Cheng had been waiting for years to balance this bloody ledger.

In Jiang Cheng's eyes, the fall of Lotus Pier wasn't just Wei Wuxian's fault—Wen Ning and Lan Wangji were just as drenched in the blame. He wouldn't give any of the three a civil word on their best day, let alone when they showed up on his doorstep together, parading around his home. The man had probably been boiling alive from the moment they set foot in Yunmeng.


A/N- The "Three Bows" (San Bai, 三拜) or kowtowing ritual is a core element of a traditional Chinese wedding ceremony (Baitang, 拜堂). 
The couple performs three specific bows during the ceremony
  • First Bow (To Heaven and Earth)
  • Second Bow (To Parents)
  • Third Bow (To Each Other)
